title: The Copper Beeches
bigQuestion: A stranger picks Violet Hunter out of a room before she has spoken, offers her three times the going rate, and will give way on everything except her hair. She says no, and then says yes. What is she like — and what has Mr. Rucastle told you about himself without meaning to?

dull.title: Holmes in an ill temper
text: It was a cold morning of the early spring, and Sherlock Holmes and I sat after breakfast on either side of a cheery fire in Baker Street.
Holmes had been silent all morning, dipping into the advertisement columns of several newspapers, until at last, giving up his search, he emerged in an ill temper.
“Watson, I fear the days of the great cases are past.”
“Man, or at least criminal man, has lost all enterprise and originality.”
“My own practice seems to be degenerating into an agency for recovering lost pencils and giving advice to young ladies from boarding-schools.”
“I think that I have touched bottom at last, however.”

zero.title: The note that marks his zero point
text: “This note I had this morning marks my zero point, I fancy. Read it!”
He tossed a crumpled letter across to me.
It was dated from Montague Place upon the preceding evening, and ran thus:
I am very anxious to consult you as to whether I should or should not accept a situation that has been offered to me as governess.
I shall call at half-past ten tomorrow, if I do not inconvenience you.

whim.title: What the blue carbuncle taught them
text: “Do you know the young lady?” I asked.
“Not I.”
“It may turn out to be of more interest than you think.”
“You remember that the affair of the blue carbuncle, which appeared to be a mere whim at first, developed into a serious investigation. It may be so in this case also.”
“Well, let us hope so! But our doubts will very soon be solved, for here, unless I am much mistaken, is the person in question.”

violet.title: A woman who has had to make her own way
text: She was plainly but neatly dressed, with a bright, quick face, freckled, and with the brisk manner of a woman who has had to make her own way in the world.
“but I have had a very strange experience, and as I have no relations from whom I could ask advice, I thought that perhaps you would be kind enough to tell me what I should do.”
“Pray take a seat, Miss Hunter. I shall be happy to do anything that I can to serve you.”
I could see that Holmes was favorably impressed by the manner of his new client.
He looked her over, in his searching fashion, and then composed himself to listen to her story.

situation.title: Out of work, and nearly out of money
text: “I have been a governess for five years,” said she, “in the family of Colonel Spence Munro.”
“Two months ago the Colonel received an appointment in Nova Scotia and took his children over to America with him, so that I found myself without a situation.”
“I advertised, but without success.”
“At last the little money that I had saved began to run short, and I was at my wits’ end as to what I should do.”

agency.title: Westaway’s, and the stout man at Miss Stoper’s elbow
text: “There is a well-known agency for governesses called Westaway’s, and there I used to call about once a week to see whether anything had turned up that might suit me.”
“Westaway was the name of the founder of the business, but it is really managed by Miss Stoper.”
“A very stout man with a smiling face, and a heavy chin, sat at her elbow with a pair of glasses on his nose, looking very earnestly at the ladies who entered.”
“As I came in he gave a jump in his chair and turned quickly to Miss Stoper:”
“That will do,” said he; “I could not ask for anything better. Capital!”

salary.title: Four pounds a month, and then a hundred a year
text: “I had four pounds a month in my last place with Colonel Spence Munro.”
“Oh, tut, tut!” he cried, throwing his fat hands out into the air. “How could anyone offer so pitiful a sum to a lady with such attractions and accomplishments?”
“The point is, have you or have you not the bearing and deportment of a lady?”
“If you have not, you are not fitted for the rearing of a child who may some day play a considerable part in the history of the country.”
“Your salary with me, madam, would begin at a hundred pounds a year.”

advance.title: Half the salary, before she has done a day of it
text: “You may imagine, Mr. Holmes, that to me, destitute as I was, such an offer seemed almost too good to be true.”
“The gentleman, however, seeing perhaps the look of disbelief upon my face, opened a wallet and took out a note.”
“It is also my custom,” said he, smiling, “to advance to my young ladies half their salary beforehand, so that they may meet any little expenses of their journey and their wardrobe.”
“It seemed to me that I had never met so thoughtful a man.”

“As I was already in debt, the advance was a great convenience, and yet there was something unnatural about the whole transaction that made me wish to know a little more before I quite committed myself.”

child.title: One dear little romper, six years old
text: “Hampshire. Charming rural place. The Copper Beeches, five miles on the far side of Winchester.”
“One child – one dear little romper just six years old. Oh, if you could see him killing cockroaches with a slipper! Smack! smack! smack! Three gone before you could wink!”
“I was a little startled at the nature of the child’s amusement, but the father’s laughter made me think that perhaps he was joking.”
“My sole duties, then,” I asked, “are to take charge of a single child?”
“Your duty would be to obey any little commands that my wife might give, provided always that they were such as a lady might with propriety obey.”

faddy.title: “We are faddy people”
text: “Quite so. In dress now, for example! We are faddy people, you know – faddy, but kindhearted.”
“If you were asked to wear any dress that we might give you, you would not object to our little whim. Heh?”
“Or to sit here, or sit there, that would not be offensive, to you?”
“Oh, no.”
“Or to cut your hair quite short before you come to us?”

hair.title: The one thing she will not do
text: “I could hardly believe my ears. As you may observe, Mr. Holmes, my hair is luxuriant, and of a peculiar tint of chestnut.”
“I could not dream of sacrificing it in this off-hand fashion.”
“I am afraid that that is quite impossible,” said I.
He had been watching me eagerly, and I could see a shadow pass over his face as I spoke.
“I am afraid that is quite essential,” said he. “It is a little fancy of my wife’s, and ladies’ fancies, you know, madam, must be consulted.”
“No, sir, I really could not,” I answered firmly.

stoper.title: A gong, and an empty cupboard
text: “Miss Stoper had sat all this while busy with her papers, but she glanced at me now with such annoyance on her face that I could not help suspecting that she had lost a handsome commission through my refusal.”
“Well, really, it seems rather useless, since you refuse the most excellent offers,” said she sharply.
“You can hardly expect us to exert ourselves to find another such opening for you.” She struck a gong, and I was shown out.
“Well, Mr. Holmes, when I got back to my lodging and found little in the cupboard, and two or three bills upon the table, I began to ask myself whether I had not done a very foolish thing.”
“Few governesses in England get a hundred a year. Besides, what use was my hair to me?”

letter2.title: The second letter, and the blue dress
text: Miss Stoper has kindly given me your address, and I write to ask whether you have reconsidered your decision.
We are willing to give thirty pounds a quarter, or £120 a year, to recompense you for any inconvenience our fads may cause you.
My wife is fond of a particular shade of electric blue and would like you to wear such a dress indoors in the morning.
You need not go to the expense of purchasing one, as we have one belonging to my dear daughter Alice (now in Philadelphia) which would, I think, fit you very well.
As regards your hair, it is no doubt a pity, especially as I could not help noticing its beauty during our interview, but I am afraid that I must remain firm upon this point.

uneasy.title: “The pay is good — too good”
text: “I confess that it is not the situation that I should like to see a sister of mine apply for.”
“Ah, I have no facts. I cannot tell. Perhaps you have yourself formed some opinion?”
“Is it not possible that his wife is a lunatic, that he desires to keep the matter quiet for fear she should be taken to an asylum, and that he humors her fancies in order to prevent an outbreak.”
“That is a possible solution – as matters stand, it is the most probable one. But in any case it does not seem to be a nice household for a young lady.”
“Yes, the pay is good – too good. That is what makes me uneasy. Why should they give £120 a year, when they could have their pick for £40?”

telegram.title: “It would cease to be a danger if we could define it”
text: “Your problem promises to be the most interesting that has come my way for some months.”
“Danger! What danger do you foresee?”
Holmes shook his head gravely. “It would cease to be a danger if we could define it,” said he. “But at any time, day or night, a telegram would bring me down to your help.”
She rose briskly from her chair, with the anxiety swept from her face.
“I shall go to Hampshire easy in my mind. I shall write to Mr. Rucastle at once, sacrifice my hair tonight, and start for Winchester tomorrow.”
“At least,” said I, “she seems to be a young lady who is able to take care of herself.”
“And she would need to be,” said Holmes gravely.

summons.title: “Do come! I am at my wits’ end”
text: “Facts! facts! facts!” he cried impatiently. “I can’t make bricks without clay.”
The telegram we eventually received came late one night, just as I was thinking of turning in, and Holmes was settling down to one of those all-night researches that he frequently indulged in.
“Just look up the trains,” said he, and turned back to his studies.
Please be at the Black Swan Hotel at Winchester at midday tomorrow. Do come! I am at my wits’ end.
By eleven o’clock the next day we were well upon our way.

freedom.title: She has her freedom, and seven explanations
text: “Well, Watson, it is clear that Miss Hunter is not personally threatened.”
“No. If she can come to Winchester to meet us, she can get away.”
“Quite so. She has her freedom.”
“I have devised seven separate explanations, each of which would cover the facts as far as we know them.”
“I will do so, and I must be quick, for I have promised Mr. Rucastle to be back before three.”
“I got his permission to come into town this morning, though he didn’t know the purpose.”

house.title: The house that gives the story its name
text: “In the first place, I have met with no actual ill treatment from Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle. It is only fair to say that.”
“But I cannot understand their reasons for their conduct.”
“It is, as he said, beautifully situated, but it is not beautiful in itself. It is a large square block of a house all stained and streaked with damp weather.”
“There are woods on three sides, and on the fourth a field slopes down to the high road.”
“A clump of copper beeches in front of the hall door has given its name to the place.”
“There was no truth, Mr. Holmes, in our conjecture. Mrs. Rucastle is not mad.”

missions.name: Section 1 — pages 165 to 167
missions.blurb: A dull morning, a letter, and what the blue carbuncle taught them

hi: emerged in an ill temper
the days of the great cases are past
recovering lost pencils
I have touched bottom at last

vs.q: What sort of mood is Holmes in at the start of the story?
opts: Cheerful, because a new case has arrived
Thoughtful, and working quietly on an old problem of his own
Out of temper, because nothing interesting is happening
Anxious about a client he is expecting
vs.why: He has spent the whole morning in the advertisement columns and found nothing, and “emerged in an ill temper.” The story opens on a bored man, which is worth remembering when he says later that this problem is the most interesting in months.

vs.q: What complaint does Holmes make about criminals?
opts: That the police catch them too easily now
That they have lost all enterprise and originality
That they have grown far more dangerous
That there are simply fewer of them than there were
vs.why: “Man, or at least criminal man, has lost all enterprise and originality.” It is a complaint about being bored, dressed up as a complaint about the world — and it tells you what Holmes actually wants from his work.

vs.q: How does Holmes describe what his practice has come down to?
opts: Work he is too proud to take on at all
A business that no longer pays its way
An agency for lost pencils and advice to schoolgirls
A series of cases the police have already solved
vs.why: “An agency for recovering lost pencils and giving advice to young ladies from boarding-schools.” Keep the second half of that in mind: a young lady is about to walk in asking for advice, and he has just called it the bottom.

vs.q: Which trait of Holmes does this opening page show most clearly?
opts: He is generous with his time
He is restless, and needs a problem to work on
He is suspicious of almost everyone he meets
He is careless about money
vs.why: Silent all morning, searching the papers, then sour when he finds nothing. The interest is not in the money or the danger — it is in having something to think about, and he is miserable without one.

vs.q: Why does the story bother to show Holmes bored before the case begins?
opts: To explain why he charges Miss Hunter nothing
To show that he is not as clever as he was
So that his interest later means something
To suggest he will refuse to take the case
vs.why: A man who calls this note his “zero point” and then says the problem is the most interesting to come his way in months has moved a long way. The boredom is there so you can measure the change.

hi: marks my zero point
a crumpled letter
a situation that has been offered to me as governess
half-past ten

vs.q: What does Holmes call the note he received that morning?
opts: His zero point
A case worth taking at once
The strangest letter he has read
A note he intends not to answer
vs.why: “This note I had this morning marks my zero point, I fancy.” The lowest his work has sunk — and he tosses it across to Watson crumpled, which says what he thought of it.

vs.q: What is the writer of the letter asking Holmes to help with?
opts: Finding a relative who has disappeared
Recovering money she is owed
Whether to accept a job as a governess
A theft from the house where she works
vs.why: “Whether I should or should not accept a situation that has been offered to me as governess.” No crime, no mystery — a woman asking advice about a job offer, which is exactly the work Holmes has just finished sneering at.

vs.q: When does the writer say she will call?
opts: That evening, after dark
At half-past ten the next morning
At noon on the following day
She asks Holmes to write to her instead
vs.why: Half-past ten — and it is half-past ten as Watson reads the letter. She arrives on the minute, which is the first thing the story tells you about her without saying it.

vs.q: What does the way she writes tell you about her?
opts: She is used to giving orders
She writes as somebody who expects to be refused
She is direct, polite, and does not waste words
She is too frightened to say what is wrong
vs.why: Four lines: what she wants, when she will come, and an apology for the trouble. “If I do not inconvenience you.” She states her business and stops, which matches the brisk woman who walks in a page later.

vs.q: Holmes calls this note the worst thing in his morning’s post. What is the reader meant to notice?
opts: That Holmes greatly dislikes writing letters
That he has misjudged it, and will find out
That the letter is badly written
That he has met the writer before
vs.why: He says so on a page that also reminds you how the blue carbuncle began. The story is telling you plainly that his first judgement is wrong, and then letting him find out.

hi: appeared to be a mere whim at first
developed into a serious investigation
It may be so in this case also

vs.q: Which earlier case does Watson bring up?
opts: The Engineer’s Thumb
The affair of the blue carbuncle
The Red-Headed League, and the pawnbroker
The Speckled Band
vs.why: The blue carbuncle — the goose, the hat and the stone. Watson has learned something from it, and the thing he has learned is the point of mentioning it here.

vs.q: What is Watson’s point in mentioning it?
opts: That Holmes was wrong about the carbuncle too
That the carbuncle case made Holmes famous
That a case which looks like a whim can turn serious
That the police were no help in that case either
vs.why: “Which appeared to be a mere whim at first, developed into a serious investigation. It may be so in this case also.” A hat on a chair became a man facing seven years. Watson is arguing from experience.

vs.q: What does this exchange show about how the two men work together?
opts: Watson usually sees further than Holmes does
Watson pushes back, and Holmes listens
Holmes refuses to discuss cases with Watson
They agree on almost everything
vs.why: Holmes has written the letter off; Watson says wait. It is the same job Watson did over the hat, when he called the whole thing a waste of energy — he is the one who makes Holmes say out loud why he thinks what he thinks.

vs.q: Who turns out to be right, Holmes or Watson?
opts: Holmes — the case stays trivial throughout
Watson — Holmes calls it the most interesting case in months
Neither — the case is never solved
Holmes — he refuses to take the case, and is proved right
vs.why: Ten pages later Holmes tells Miss Hunter her problem “promises to be the most interesting that has come my way for some months.” Watson said it would be, and it was.

vs.q: What is a reader meant to do with this reminder of an earlier case?
opts: Skip ahead to see how this one ends
Expect the two cases to have the same solution
Take the small, odd details in this one seriously
Assume Miss Hunter is not telling the truth
vs.why: In the carbuncle it was a hat nobody wanted. Here it will be a dress, a chair, and a haircut. The story is teaching you how to read it: the trivial detail is where the case is.

missions.name: Section 2 — pages 167 to 169
missions.blurb: Who Violet Hunter is, and why she needs the work

hi: plainly but neatly dressed
make her own way in the world
no relations from whom I could ask advice
favorably impressed

vs.q: How is Miss Hunter described when she comes in?
opts: Expensively dressed, and sure of herself
Plainly but neatly dressed, with a bright, quick face
Pale and frightened, hardly able to speak
Older than Holmes had expected her, and very grave
vs.why: Plain and neat, bright and quick, freckled. Not a rich client and not a helpless one — Watson's description tells you her situation and her character in one sentence.

vs.q: What does Watson mean by “the brisk manner of a woman who has had to make her own way in the world”?
opts: That she is rude to people she does not know
That she has supported herself, and it shows
That she walks very quickly
That she has travelled a great deal
vs.why: Nobody has done it for her. The briskness is what five years of earning her own living has made of her, and Watson can see it before she has said twenty words.

vs.q: Why has she come to a stranger for advice?
opts: Her employer told her to consult Holmes
She suspects a crime has been committed
She has no relations she could ask
She has read about Holmes in the newspapers
vs.why: “As I have no relations from whom I could ask advice.” She is entirely alone, which is the thing that makes the rest of the story possible — and which she states plainly rather than complaining about.

vs.q: How does Holmes receive her?
opts: Coldly, since he had called her letter his zero point
He is favorably impressed by her manner
He keeps her waiting while he finishes the papers
He tells her at once that he cannot help
vs.why: “I could see that Holmes was favorably impressed by the manner of his new client.” The man who was sour about schoolgirls asking advice rises to greet her and offers her a chair. The person, not the letter, changes his mind.

vs.q: Which two traits does this first description give Miss Hunter?
opts: Wealth and confidence
Nervousness and suspicion
Independence and good sense
Pride and bad temper
vs.why: She makes her own living and she knows when to ask for help — and she asks the right person. Watch how those two hold up through the rest of the reading, because they are tested on every page.

hi: a governess for five years
Colonel Spence Munro
without a situation
at my wits’ end

vs.q: How long had Miss Hunter been a governess, and for whom?
opts: Two years, for Mr. Rucastle
Five years, for Colonel Spence Munro
Ten years, for several families
One year, in her first position
vs.why: Five years with one family. She is experienced and she stayed, which tells you she was good at it and that they wanted to keep her.

vs.q: Why did she lose her position?
opts: She was dismissed after a disagreement
She left to care for a relative
The Colonel took a post in Nova Scotia and took the children
The family could no longer afford to keep a governess at all
vs.why: Nothing to do with her. The family went to America and the job went with them, which is worth noticing — the story is careful that her trouble is bad luck rather than any fault of hers.

vs.q: What had she done about finding another position?
opts: Waited for the family to send for her
Advertised, without success
Written to every family she knew
Nothing — she had savings to live on
vs.why: “I advertised, but without success.” She tried the obvious thing first and it failed. The agency and then the interview are what she does next, which is the shape of the whole first half of her story.

vs.q: What state were her finances in by the time she reached Westaway’s?
opts: Comfortable, with a year’s savings
She had enough to last the winter
Her savings were running short and she was at her wits’ end
She was still being supported by Colonel Spence Munro
vs.why: Her savings running out and no work. Remember it: every strange condition she is about to be offered has to be weighed against an empty cupboard, and the story makes sure you know that first.

vs.q: Why does the story give her money troubles before the offer is made?
opts: To show she is bad with money
To explain why she accepted the job
To make the reader doubt her account
To explain why she cannot pay Holmes
vs.why: A hundred pounds a year means nothing until you know she has two bills on the table and little in the cupboard. Her decision looks foolish without that and reasonable with it, and Doyle puts it first on purpose.

hi: a well-known agency for governesses called Westaway’s
it is really managed by Miss Stoper
A very stout man with a smiling face, and a heavy chin
I could not ask for anything better

vs.q: What is Westaway’s?
opts: The house where she had been a governess
An agency that finds positions for governesses
The firm that employed Colonel Spence Munro
The newspaper where she placed her advertisement
vs.why: An agency, called after its founder but run by Miss Stoper. Governesses waited in an outer room to be shown in one at a time — which is how a stranger comes to be sitting there watching them arrive.

vs.q: Who was sitting at Miss Stoper’s elbow when Miss Hunter was shown in?
opts: Another governess, waiting her turn to be seen
Mr. Westaway, the founder
A clerk writing in the ledgers
A very stout man with a heavy chin and glasses
vs.why: A stranger, in the office where the employer should not be, “looking very earnestly at the ladies who entered.” He is inspecting them as they come in, one by one.

vs.q: What did the stout man do the moment she came in?
opts: He rose and introduced himself politely
He gave a jump in his chair and said “That will do”
He asked Miss Stoper to show him all of her ledgers
He looked away and said nothing at all
vs.why: “That will do; I could not ask for anything better. Capital!” Before a word has passed between them. He has decided on sight, which means he was looking for something he could see.

vs.q: What is odd about his deciding before she has spoken?
opts: It means he had met her somewhere before
It means Miss Stoper had recommended her
It means he wants something about her appearance
It means that he was in a great hurry to leave
vs.why: An employer hiring a governess asks about teaching. This one jumps in his chair at the sight of her and asks about salary. Everything he later insists on — the dress, the chair, the hair — is about how she looks.

vs.q: Which detail of this scene turns out to matter most later?
opts: That the agency is named after its founder
That the ladies waited in an outside room
That Miss Stoper consults her ledgers
That he chose her by looking at her
vs.why: He is not hiring a teacher. He is choosing someone who will do for a purpose he has not mentioned, and the choosing is done with his eyes before she has opened her mouth.

missions.name: Section 3 — pages 170 to 172
missions.blurb: The offer: a hundred a year, and half of it in advance

hi: four pounds a month
so pitiful a sum
the bearing and deportment of a lady
a hundred pounds a year

vs.q: What had Miss Hunter been paid in her last position?
opts: Rather more than most governesses got
Thirty pounds a quarter
Four pounds a month
She does not say what it was
vs.why: Four pounds a month — about forty-eight pounds a year. Hold the number: everything the stranger offers has to be measured against it.

vs.q: How does the stout man react to that figure?
opts: He says it is a fair wage for the work
He calls it a pitiful sum and throws his hands in the air
He says that he can offer her only a little more than that
He asks what her duties had been for it
vs.why: “How could anyone offer so pitiful a sum to a lady with such attractions and accomplishments?” He is insulting her last employer to flatter her, and she has not asked him for anything.

vs.q: What does he say is the real question about a governess?
opts: What she can teach, and how well
How long she stayed in her last position
Whether she has the bearing and deportment of a lady
Whether she is willing to live far from London
vs.why: “Have you or have you not the bearing and deportment of a lady? There it is in a nutshell.” Bearing and deportment — how she carries herself. Not one word about lessons, in the whole interview.

vs.q: What salary does he finally name?
opts: Forty pounds a year
Four pounds a month, as before
A hundred pounds a year
Thirty pounds a quarter
vs.why: A hundred a year — more than double what she had. She says later that few governesses in England get it, and she is right, which is exactly what should have worried her.

vs.q: When Miss Hunter says her accomplishments may be less than he imagines, what does he do?
opts: Asks her to list them in detail
Waves it aside as beside the question
Lowers the salary he had offered
Says he will test her on them
vs.why: “Tut, tut! This is all quite beside the question.” She is being honest about what she can do and he does not want to hear it — because her accomplishments are not what he is buying.

hi: destitute as I was
opened a wallet and took out a note
half their salary beforehand
something unnatural about the whole transaction

vs.q: What does the stout man offer when he sees her look of disbelief?
opts: To put the offer in writing
To let her meet the child first
Half her salary in advance
To pay her travelling costs himself
vs.why: He opens a wallet and takes out a note. “It is also my custom to advance to my young ladies half their salary beforehand.” Fifty pounds, to a woman who has nothing, for work she has not begun.

vs.q: What reason does he give for the advance?
opts: That he always pays before work is done
So she can meet the expenses of her journey and her wardrobe
That the bank is a very long way away from the house itself
To make up for the loss of her hair
vs.why: Journey and wardrobe. Notice the second one: he is already paying for what she will wear, several minutes before he mentions that his wife chooses her dresses.

vs.q: What was Miss Hunter’s first reaction to the advance?
opts: That she had never met so thoughtful a man
That it proved he could not be trusted
That it was less than she had hoped for
That she should ask for the rest as well
vs.why: “It seemed to me that I had never met so thoughtful a man.” She is in debt and somebody has just solved it. The story lets her be grateful before it lets her be suspicious.

vs.q: And what did she think on top of that?
opts: That she would accept at once
That the money would clear every one of her debts entirely
That there was something unnatural about the whole transaction
That he had mistaken her for someone else
vs.why: Both things at once — grateful and uneasy. “Something unnatural about the whole transaction that made me wish to know a little more before I quite committed myself.” That instinct is the best thing about her.

vs.q: What trait is she showing by asking more questions when the money is already on the table?
opts: Greed — she wants a better offer
Caution — she will not be bought past her own judgement
Rudeness — she does not trust a stranger with money
Fear — she expects to be cheated
vs.why: A woman in debt with fifty pounds in front of her keeps asking. It would have been so much easier to take it and stop talking, and she does not.

hi: five miles on the far side of Winchester
killing cockroaches with a slipper
startled at the nature of the child’s amusement
obey any little commands that my wife might give

vs.q: Where is the house, and what is it called?
opts: Montague Place, in London
The Copper Beeches, five miles beyond Winchester
Westaway’s, near the agency
Nova Scotia, with the Spence Munro family and the children
vs.why: The Copper Beeches, in Hampshire, five miles on the far side of Winchester. The name comes from a clump of trees by the front door, as she finds out when she gets there.

vs.q: How does the father describe his six-year-old son?
opts: As a quiet child who reads a great deal and gives no trouble
As delicate, and often ill
As a dear little romper who kills cockroaches with a slipper
As too young yet to need a governess
vs.why: “Smack! smack! smack! Three gone before you could wink!” He tells it as a joke about his own child, laughing, to a woman he is trying to hire.

vs.q: How does Miss Hunter take that description?
opts: She laughs along with the father
She is startled, but thinks he may be joking
She refuses the position on the spot
She asks to meet the child before deciding
vs.why: “I was a little startled at the nature of the child’s amusement, but the father’s laughter made me think that perhaps he was joking.” She notices and then explains it away — which is what people do when they need the work.

vs.q: What does he say her duties will be, besides the child?
opts: Teaching French and music
Keeping all of the household accounts in order
Obeying any little commands his wife might give
Nothing else at all
vs.why: “Provided always that they were such as a lady might with propriety obey.” The qualification sounds reassuring and is not: he is telling her in advance that she will be asked to do things that need a promise attached.

vs.q: Three things in this exchange should worry a reader. Which is NOT one of them?
opts: A child whose amusement is killing things
Duties that are deliberately left vague
A house in the country five miles from a town
A father who laughs at his son’s cruelty
vs.why: Living in the country is ordinary; a governess post almost always meant living in. The other three are not ordinary, and all three are offered cheerfully, which is what makes them hard to object to.

missions.name: Section 4 — pages 173 to 174
missions.blurb: The one condition she refuses, and what refusing costs her

hi: We are faddy people
wear any dress that we might give you
Or to sit here, or sit there
cut your hair quite short before you come to us

vs.q: What word does the stout man use for his family’s odd requests?
opts: Rules
Fads — they are faddy people
Traditions
Conditions of employment
vs.why: “We are faddy people, you know – faddy, but kindhearted.” A fad is a harmless little preference. The word is doing a great deal of work, and it is the word he keeps coming back to.

vs.q: What three things does he ask her to agree to?
opts: To teach only in the mornings, to live in, and to travel with them
To wear a dress they give her, to sit where she is told, to cut her hair
To keep accounts, to answer the door, to cut her hair
To wear black, to rise early, to stay indoors
vs.why: Dress, position, hair. Each is asked separately and each sounds smaller than the one before — and together they amount to controlling exactly how she looks and where she can be seen.

vs.q: Why does he put the requests in that order?
opts: He is working through them as he thinks of them
He asks the costly ones first to get them over with
Each small yes makes the next one easier to give
His wife had written the order down for him
vs.why: A dress, then a chair, then her hair. She says yes, yes — and then he asks for the thing he actually came for. By then she has already agreed twice.

vs.q: What does “faddy, but kindhearted” do for him?
opts: It explains why the salary is so high
It makes strange demands sound harmless
It warns her that the family is difficult
It is a joke at his wife’s expense
vs.why: Nobody argues with kindhearted. He is giving her the words to explain the demands away with, and she uses them: she talks herself round twice in the next two pages.

vs.q: Which demand is the one he really wants?
opts: The dress
Where she sits
Her hair
All three equally
vs.why: It is the only one he will not drop. When she refuses, the interview ends — and when he writes again he gives way on nothing else and stays “firm upon this point.”

hi: my hair is luxuriant, and of a peculiar tint of chestnut
quite impossible
a shadow pass over his face
I answered firmly

vs.q: What is Miss Hunter’s hair like?
opts: Cut short already
Fair, and always worn pinned up in a long plait
Luxuriant, and of a peculiar tint of chestnut
Grey before its time
vs.why: Luxuriant and a peculiar chestnut. Peculiar means unusual. It is the one thing about her anyone would describe first — which is the whole reason it is being asked for.

vs.q: How does she answer the request to cut it?
opts: She says she will think it over
She says it is quite impossible, and then firmly refuses
She agrees, since the salary is so high
She asks whether a wig would not do just as well instead
vs.why: “I am afraid that that is quite impossible… No, sir, I really could not,” I answered firmly. Twice, and the second time with no softening at all.

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter notice on his face as she refuses?
opts: A smile he was trying to hide
Nothing — he did not react at all
A shadow passing over it
That he had stopped listening
vs.why: “He had been watching me eagerly, and I could see a shadow pass over his face.” Watching eagerly, before she answers. This matters more to him than anything he has said aloud.

vs.q: Whose idea is the haircut supposed to be?
opts: His own
A little fancy of his wife’s
His daughter Alice’s own
Miss Stoper’s
vs.why: “It is a little fancy of my wife’s, and ladies’ fancies, you know, madam, must be consulted.” He puts it on somebody who is not in the room, which means it cannot be argued with and he need not defend it.

vs.q: What does refusing show about her, given what we know of her situation?
opts: That she does not really need the money
That she is vain about her appearance
That there is a line she will not cross for money
That she did not believe the offer was real
vs.why: She has two bills on her table and almost nothing saved, and she is being offered four times her old salary. She says no anyway, firmly, and then has to go home and live with it.

hi: lost a handsome commission
it seems rather useless
She struck a gong
what use was my hair to me

vs.q: How does Miss Stoper behave after the refusal?
opts: She takes Miss Hunter’s side against the gentleman
She is annoyed, and says it is useless keeping her name
She offers to find her another position at once
She says nothing at all about it
vs.why: She glances up “with such annoyance on her face” that Miss Hunter suspects she has lost a handsome commission. The agency is paid when a place is filled, so the refusal costs her money.

vs.q: How does the interview end?
opts: Miss Stoper strikes a gong and Miss Hunter is shown out
The gentleman apologises and leaves
Miss Hunter changes her mind and accepts
Miss Stoper agrees to go on looking for something else
vs.why: A gong, and out. Nothing is said about finding her anything else — in fact she is told she can hardly expect them to exert themselves. She has made an enemy of the agency by having a limit.

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter find when she gets back to her lodging?
opts: A letter from Colonel Spence Munro
Little in the cupboard and two or three bills on the table
A note from Mr. Rucastle already waiting on the table
That her rent had been paid for her
vs.why: An empty cupboard and bills. The story puts this straight after the refusal on purpose: it shows you exactly what the principle cost, in the same hour she paid it.

vs.q: How does she come to feel about her refusal over the next two days?
opts: More certain than ever that she was right
That she had done a very foolish thing
That she should report the man to the police
That the offer had never been serious
vs.why: By the next day she was inclined to think she had made a mistake, “and by the day after I was sure of it.” Hunger is an argument, and she says so honestly instead of pretending she was brave all through.

vs.q: “Besides, what use was my hair to me?” What is she doing in that sentence?
opts: Telling Holmes she never liked her hair
Explaining why the first refusal was right
Talking herself out of her own objection
Repeating something Miss Stoper had said
vs.why: She is arguing herself round, and she knows it well enough to repeat the argument to Holmes. The honesty of telling him how she changed her mind is what makes her worth believing about everything else.

missions.name: Section 5 — pages 175 to 179
missions.blurb: The second letter, and the thing that makes Holmes uneasy

hi: thirty pounds a quarter
inconvenience our fads may cause you
a particular shade of electric blue
my dear daughter Alice (now in Philadelphia)

vs.q: What does the second letter offer her?
opts: The same hundred pounds, and no conditions
£120 a year, to recompense her for the fads
Her old salary of four pounds a month
A trial month before anything is decided
vs.why: Thirty pounds a quarter — £120 a year. He has raised it again without being asked, and he says plainly what the extra is for: “to recompense you for any inconvenience our fads may cause you.”

vs.q: What does the letter say about the dress?
opts: That she must buy one for herself in London before she comes down
That his wife likes electric blue, and they already have such a dress
That she may wear whatever she pleases indoors
That the dress is to be worn only for visitors
vs.why: A particular shade of electric blue, to be worn indoors in the morning — and she need not buy one, because they have one already. A dress waiting in the house before the governess has agreed to come.

vs.q: Whose dress is it?
opts: Mrs. Rucastle’s own
One bought for the last governess they had
His daughter Alice’s, now in Philadelphia
The letter does not say
vs.why: Alice Rucastle’s, “now in Philadelphia” — the first time anyone mentions a daughter. A dress belonging to a young woman who has gone away, and it is expected to fit Miss Hunter.

vs.q: What does the letter not give way on?
opts: The salary
The dress
Where she is to sit
Her hair
vs.why: “I am afraid that I must remain firm upon this point.” He pays more, he supplies the dress, he calls the duties light — and the one thing he will not move on is the haircut.

vs.q: Who is the letter signed by?
opts: Miss Stoper
Jephro Rucastle
Colonel Spence Munro
Alice Rucastle
vs.why: Jephro Rucastle — the first time the stout man is given a name, several pages after we met him. Until this letter he has simply been the gentleman in Miss Stoper’s office.

hi: a sister of mine
I have no facts. I cannot tell
his wife is a lunatic
the pay is good – too good

vs.q: What does Holmes say when she asks whether she should refuse?
opts: That she must certainly refuse
That it is not a place he would like a sister of his to apply for
That the decision is hers alone, and he will not comment on it
That the family sound perfectly respectable
vs.why: “I confess that it is not the situation that I should like to see a sister of mine apply for.” As strong a warning as he can give without facts — and he still does not tell her what to do.

vs.q: When she asks what it all means, what does Holmes answer?
opts: That the wife is certainly mad
That Mr. Rucastle is plainly a criminal
That he has no facts, and cannot tell
That the dress is the key to the whole thing
vs.why: “Ah, I have no facts. I cannot tell.” The same answer he gave about Horner. He will say what he knows and no more, which is why it is worth something when he does say a thing.

vs.q: What is Miss Hunter’s own explanation?
opts: That the family want her for her hair
That Mr. Rucastle’s wife is mad, and he is humouring her
That they mean to rob her of the advance
That the child is dangerous and the parents both know it
vs.why: A wife he keeps from an asylum by giving in to her fancies. Holmes calls it “the most probable one” as matters stand — and she finds out herself, when she gets there, that it is wrong.

vs.q: What is the one thing that makes Holmes uneasy?
opts: That the house is far from London
That nobody has met the wife
That the pay is too good
That Miss Stoper was annoyed
vs.why: “Why should they give £120 a year, when they could have their pick for £40?” Everybody else is pleased about the money. Holmes asks what is being bought with it, which is not the same question.

vs.q: Why is “the pay is good – too good” a piece of reasoning rather than a feeling?
opts: Because Holmes has met Mr. Rucastle before
Because the market price of the work is known, and this is triple it
Because Miss Hunter had already said very much the same thing herself
Because the advance was paid in cash
vs.why: Governesses could be had for £40. Paying three times the going rate means paying for something besides the work — he does not yet know what, and he says so, but the gap itself is the evidence.

hi: the most interesting that has come my way
It would cease to be a danger if we could define it
She rose briskly from her chair
able to take care of herself

vs.q: What does Holmes now say about her problem?
opts: That it is too slight to be worth his time
That it is the most interesting to come his way in months
That he will take it only if she is paid in advance
That the police should be told at once
vs.why: The man who called her letter his zero point. Watson was right on page 167, and this is the sentence that proves it.

vs.q: When she asks what danger he foresees, what does he say?
opts: That the child is the danger
That he fears for her hair, and for nothing else at all
That it would cease to be a danger if they could define it
That there is no danger at all
vs.why: A danger you can name is one you can guard against. He cannot name this one, which is exactly why it worries him — and it is the most honest thing he could have said.

vs.q: What does he promise her?
opts: To come down if she telegraphs, day or night
To write to Mr. Rucastle on her behalf
To send Watson with her to Hampshire
To find her another position if this fails
vs.why: “At any time, day or night, a telegram would bring me down to your help.” It is the whole of what he can offer, and it turns out to be enough — she leaves with the anxiety swept from her face.

vs.q: What does she say she will do that night?
opts: Write to Colonel Spence Munro
Go back to Miss Stoper
Sacrifice her hair
Think it over once more
vs.why: “I shall write to Mr. Rucastle at once, sacrifice my hair tonight, and start for Winchester tomorrow.” Decided, and then done the same evening. The word sacrifice says what it costs her and she does it anyway.

vs.q: Watson says she can take care of herself. What does Holmes reply, and what does it mean?
opts: “And she would need to be” — he expects her to need it
That she is braver than she is sensible
That she will not last a single week in that house
That Watson is too easily impressed
vs.why: “And she would need to be,” said Holmes gravely. It is agreement and a warning in five words — and the reading breaks on it, so you are left holding it for two weeks of story time.

missions.name: Section 6 — pages 180 to 183
missions.blurb: The telegram, the Black Swan, the house — and what she is made of

hi: I can’t make bricks without clay
Just look up the trains
the Black Swan Hotel at Winchester
I am at my wits’ end

vs.q: What does Holmes say when Watson raises the case during the two weeks of waiting?
opts: That he has already solved it
“Facts! facts! facts! I can’t make bricks without clay”
That he has forgotten all about Miss Hunter
That they should go down to Hampshire without being asked
vs.why: He sits for half an hour at a time with knitted brows and then waves the subject away. He is not ignoring it — he is refusing to guess, which is a different thing and harder.

vs.q: When does the telegram arrive?
opts: The morning after she leaves
Two weeks later, late at night
A month later, by the first post
It never arrives; they go down unasked
vs.why: Two weeks, late one night, just as Watson was thinking of turning in. Long enough for the reader to wonder, which is what the two weeks are for.

vs.q: What does the telegram ask?
opts: That Holmes write to Mr. Rucastle at once
That he send a doctor to the house
That he be at the Black Swan at Winchester at midday
That he come down to the Copper Beeches after dark
vs.why: “Please be at the Black Swan Hotel at Winchester at midday tomorrow. Do come! I am at my wits’ end.” Twenty words, and two of them — “Do come!” — are not the brisk woman who left Baker Street.

vs.q: How does Holmes react to it?
opts: He telegraphs back for more detail
He says “Just look up the trains” and returns to his work
He refuses to go until morning
He wakes Watson and leaves for Hampshire immediately
vs.why: No surprise and no discussion. He had said a telegram would bring him down day or night, and when it comes he treats going as settled and gets back to what he was doing.

vs.q: She uses the phrase “at my wits’ end” twice in this story. When was the first time?
opts: When she refused to cut her hair
When her savings ran out and she had no work
When she first caught sight of the Copper Beeches
When Miss Stoper struck the gong
vs.why: On page 168, about being out of work and nearly out of money. The same five words, and the second time she is not short of money at all — which tells you how much worse this is.

hi: not personally threatened
She has her freedom
seven separate explanations
he didn’t know the purpose

vs.q: What does Holmes conclude from the fact that she can meet them in Winchester?
opts: That she is not in any real trouble
That she is not personally threatened, and has her freedom
That the Rucastles must already have dismissed her from the house
That she has left the house for good
vs.why: A prisoner cannot catch a train. It narrows the problem a great deal without solving any of it — whatever is wrong at that house, it is not being done to her.

vs.q: How many explanations has Holmes worked out on the way down?
opts: None — he still has no facts
One, which he is sure of
Three, and he favours the first
Seven, each of which fits the facts
vs.why: “Seven separate explanations, each of which would cover the facts as far as we know them.” Not one theory defended — seven held loosely, waiting for the fact that will kill six of them.

vs.q: Why is Miss Hunter in a hurry at the Black Swan?
opts: She has a train to catch back to London
She has promised Mr. Rucastle to be back before three
She is afraid of being followed
The inn is about to close up its dining room for the day
vs.why: She asked permission to come into town and has to be back by three. She is keeping her word to a man she has telegraphed Sherlock Holmes about, which is very like her.

vs.q: What has she not told Mr. Rucastle?
opts: That she went into Winchester at all
That she has written to Holmes before
The purpose of her visit to town
That she means to leave the position
vs.why: “I got his permission to come into town this morning, though he didn’t know the purpose.” She asks rather than sneaks, and keeps back only the one thing she must. Careful, not deceitful.

vs.q: What does Holmes mean by “Let us have everything in its due order”?
opts: That she should tell only what she thinks important
That she should start at the beginning and leave nothing out
That she should write it down instead of speaking
That he will ask the questions, and she should only answer
vs.why: He stretches his legs to the fire and composes himself to listen. He wants the whole thing in sequence, because he does not yet know which part matters — the same reason he says later that he is glad of all details.

hi: no actual ill treatment
stained and streaked with damp weather
A clump of copper beeches in front of the hall door
Mrs. Rucastle is not mad

vs.q: What is the first thing Miss Hunter says about the Rucastles?
opts: That they have treated her cruelly
That she has had no actual ill treatment from them
That she is frightened of both of them
That she has barely seen them since she arrived
vs.why: “I have met with no actual ill treatment from Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle. It is only fair to say that.” She has telegraphed for a detective and she still opens by being fair to them.

vs.q: What is the house itself like?
opts: Small and neat, newly built
A ruin, with half its roof gone
A large square block, stained and streaked with damp
A pretty cottage standing among the woods on three sides
vs.why: “Beautifully situated, but it is not beautiful in itself.” Woods on three sides and a field sloping to the road on the fourth — lovely country, and an ugly damp-stained house sitting in the middle of it.

vs.q: Where does the house get its name?
opts: From the Rucastle family motto
From a village of that name nearby
From a clump of copper beeches in front of the hall door
From the colour of the stone that the walls are built of
vs.why: A clump of copper beeches by the front door. The trees give the story its title, and they are the first thing you see when you arrive and the last thing between the house and the road.

vs.q: What had Miss Hunter and Holmes both guessed wrong?
opts: That the child would be difficult
That the salary would not be paid
That Mrs. Rucastle was mad
That the house would be far from Winchester
vs.why: “There was no truth, Mr. Holmes, in our conjecture. Mrs. Rucastle is not mad.” The most probable solution, held by both of them, and the first fact she brings knocks it down — which is what facts are for.

vs.q: What does “It is only fair to say that” tell you about the way she gives evidence?
opts: She is afraid of being overheard
She is trying to protect her employers
She separates what frightens her from what she can prove
She does not really believe that anything is wrong there
vs.why: She is frightened enough to send a telegram and careful enough not to let the fright do her reporting for her. That is why Holmes can use what she tells him.

hi: no actual ill treatment
It is only fair to say that
But I cannot understand their reasons for their conduct

vs.q: Across the whole reading, which set of traits best describes Violet Hunter?
opts: Timid, obedient, and easily frightened
Clever but dishonest, and out for the money
Independent, honest about herself, and firm when it matters
Proud, stubborn, and quite unwilling to take any advice
vs.why: She keeps herself, she asks for help when she needs it, she admits she nearly changed her mind for the money, she refuses the one thing she will not do — and then she does it when she has decided to go. All four show up in the pages you have just read.

vs.q: Which moment shows her courage most clearly?
opts: Refusing to cut her hair when she was almost penniless
Writing to Sherlock Holmes for advice
Travelling to Winchester to meet Holmes
Telling Mr. Rucastle she would take the position
vs.why: Two bills on the table, an empty cupboard, and four times her old salary on the other side of it. Courage is not the absence of need — it is a limit that holds when the need is real.

vs.q: She first refuses to cut her hair and later sacrifices it. Is that a change of character?
opts: Yes — she gives in as soon as the money is raised
No — refusing an order is not the same as choosing
Yes — she had always meant to accept
No — she never cuts it at all
vs.why: The first time it was a condition pressed on her in a room by a stranger, and she said no. The second time she had weighed it, decided to go, and did it herself that night. Same person, different question.

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter do that Mr. Rucastle never does?
opts: Keep a promise she has made
Say plainly what she thinks of someone
Admit when she has been wrong or uncertain
Ask for advice from a friend
vs.why: She tells Holmes she was startled, that she nearly went back, that she cannot understand the Rucastles, and that they have not ill-treated her. Rucastle is certain about everything, flatters, laughs, and never gives a reason that is really his.

vs.q: Holmes said she would need to be able to take care of herself. What in this reading suggests she can?
opts: That she took the highest salary that she had ever been offered
That she told the Rucastles nothing about Holmes
That she asked leave to go to town, went, and will be back by three
That she travelled to Hampshire alone
vs.why: She got out, got advice, and is going back — without lying, without panicking, and inside the time she promised. She is managing a frightening house rather than running from it or ignoring it.

title: The Room at the End of the Passage
bigQuestion: Violet Hunter is dressed in another woman’s clothes, sat with her back to a window, and made to laugh. Then she finds her own hair in a drawer she has never opened. What has she worked out by the end of tonight’s reading, and what is she still only guessing at?

servants.title: Two servants, and only two
text: One unpleasant thing about the house, which struck me at once, was the appearance and conduct of the servants.
There are only two, a man and his wife.
Toller, for that’s his name, is a rough, uncouth man, with grizzled hair and whiskers, and a perpetual smell of drink.
Twice since I have been with them he has been drunk, and yet Mr. Rucastle seemed to take no notice of it.
Toller’s wife is a tall and strong woman with a sour face, as silent as Mrs. Rucastle, and much less amiable.

dress.title: The blue dress, and the chair at the window
text: “We shall now see how the electric blue dress will become you. You will find it laid upon the bed in your room, and if you would put it on, we should both be extremely obliged.”
The dress I found waiting for me was of a peculiar shade of blue. It was of excellent material, but it bore unmistakable signs of having been worn before.
It could not have been a better fit if I had been measured for it.
A chair had been placed close to the central window, with its back turned towards it.
I was asked to sit, and then Mr. Rucastle, walking up and down on the other side of the room, began to tell me the funniest stories that I have ever listened to.
Mrs. Rucastle, however, never so much as smiled, but sat with her hands in her lap, and a sad, anxious look upon her face.

reading.title: The same performance, twice
text: Two days later this same performance was gone through under exactly similar circumstances.
Again I changed my dress, again I sat in the window, and again I laughed heartily at the funny stories of which my employer had an immense collection, and which he told most skillfully.
Then he handed me a novel, and, moving my chair a little sideways, begged me to read aloud to him.
I read for about ten minutes; then he ordered me to cease and change my dress.

mirror.title: A piece of broken glass in a handkerchief
text: They were always careful to turn my face away from the window, so that I became consumed with the desire to see what was going on behind my back.
My hand mirror had been broken, so I concealed a little of the glass in my handkerchief.
On the next occasion, in the midst of my laughter, I put my handkerchief up to my eyes and was able to see all there was behind me.
There was nothing.
At the second glance, however, I saw a man standing in the road, a small bearded man in a grey suit, who seemed to be looking in my direction.
This man, however, was leaning against the railings that bordered our field and was looking earnestly.

blind.title: “Kindly turn round and wave him away”
text: I lowered my handkerchief and glanced at Mrs. Rucastle, to find her eyes fixed upon me with a searching gaze.
“Jephro,” said she, “there is a fellow upon the road who stares up at Miss Hunter.”
“No friend of yours, Miss Hunter?” he asked.
“Dear me! How very impertinent! Kindly turn round and motion him to go away.”
“Surely it would be better to take no notice?”
I did as I was told, and Mrs. Rucastle drew down the blind.
That was a week ago, and from that time I have not sat in the window, nor worn the blue dress, nor seen the man in the road.

carlo.title: Carlo, loose every night
text: As we approached it, I heard the rattling of a chain and the sound of a large animal moving.
“It’s only Carlo, my mastiff. I call him mine, but really old Toller is the only man who can do anything with him.”
“We feed him once a day, and not too much then, so that he is always keen.”
“Toller lets him loose every night. God help the trespasser whom he lays his fangs upon. For goodness’ sake don’t ever set your foot over the threshold at night.”
As it emerged into the moonshine I saw it was a giant dog, as large as a calf, with hanging jowl, black muzzle, and huge bones.
That dreadful sight sent a chill to my heart, which I do not think any burglar could have done.

hair.title: Her own hair, in a drawer she had never opened
text: I had, as you know, cut off my hair in London, and I had placed it in a great coil at the bottom of my trunk.
There was an old chest of drawers in the room, the two upper ones empty and open, the lower one locked.
The very first key fit to perfection, and I drew the drawer open. There was only one thing in it, but I am sure that you would never guess what it was. It was my coil of hair.
It was of the same peculiar tint and the same thickness.
With trembling hands I undid my trunk and drew from the bottom my own hair. I laid the two tresses together, and I assure you they were identical.
I returned the strange hair to the drawer, and I said nothing of the matter to the Rucastles, as I felt that I had put myself in the wrong by opening a drawer that they had locked.

wing.title: The wing nobody lives in
text: I am naturally observant, Mr. Holmes, and I soon had a pretty good plan of the whole house in my head.
There was one wing, however, that appeared not to be inhabited.

One day, however, as I ascended the stair, I met Mr. Rucastle coming out this door, his keys in his hand, and a look on his face that made him a very different person from the jovial man to whom I was accustomed.
His cheeks were red, his brow was all crinkled with anger, and the veins stood out at his temples.
There were four, three of which were simply dirty. The fourth was shuttered up.

darkroom.title: “Photography is one of my hobbies”
text: “Photography is one of my hobbies,” said he. “I have made my darkroom up there. But, dear me! what an observant young lady we have come upon.”
He spoke in a jesting tone, but there was no jest in his eyes as he looked at me. I read suspicion there, and annoyance, but no jest.
It was not mere curiosity. It was more a feeling of duty – a feeling that some good might come from my penetrating to this place.
I once saw him carry a large black linen bag through the door.
Recently he has been drinking hard, and yesterday evening he was very drunk.

barricade.title: A bar from an iron bed, padlocked across a door
text: Round this corner were three doors in a line, the first and third of which were open. They each led into an empty room, dusty and cheerless.
The center door was closed, and across it had been fastened one of the broad bars of an iron bed, padlocked at one end to a ring in the wall, and fastened at the other with heavy cord.
This barricaded door corresponded clearly with the shuttered window outside.
I could see by the glimmer from beneath it that the room was not in darkness. Evidently a skylight let in light from above.
I suddenly heard the sound of steps within the room and saw a shadow pass back and forth against the slit of dim light that shone out from under the door.
A mad, unreasoning terror rose up in me at the sight, Mr. Holmes. My nerves failed me, and I turned and ran.

coaxing.title: A voice just a little too coaxing
text: “So,” said he, smiling, “it was you, then. I thought it must be when I saw the door open.”
But his voice was just a little too coaxing. He overdid it. I was keenly on my guard against him.
“I was foolish enough to go into the empty wing,” I answered. “But it is so lonely and eerie that I was frightened. It is so dreadfully still there!”
“Only that?” said he, looking at me keenly.
“Why do you think that I lock this door?”
“It is to keep people out who have no business there. Do you see?” He was still smiling in the most amiable manner.

mastiff.title: “I’ll throw you to the mastiff”
text: “And if you put your foot over that threshold again” – instantly the smile hardened into a grin of rage, and he glared down at me, “I’ll throw you to the mastiff.”
I was so terrified that I rushed past him into my room.
I remember nothing until I found myself lying on my bed trembling all over.
Then I thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not live there longer without some advice.
I was frightened of the house, of the man, of the woman, of the servants, even of the child. They were all horrible to me.
Of course I might have fled, but my curiosity was almost as strong as my fears.

missions.name: Section 1 — pages 185 to 186
missions.blurb: Two servants, a borrowed dress, and a chair with its back to the window

hi: There are only two, a man and his wife
a perpetual smell of drink
Mr. Rucastle seemed to take no notice of it
a tall and strong woman with a sour face

vs.q: How many servants are there at the Copper Beeches?
opts: A full household of eight or nine
Four, counting the gardener
Only two, a man and his wife
None at all; Mrs. Rucastle keeps the house herself
vs.why: Two servants for a large country house. That is remarkably few, and it is the first thing about the place that strikes her as unpleasant — a house with almost nobody in it.

vs.q: What is Toller like?
opts: Quiet, neat and very correct
Young, and quite new to the household here
Cheerful, and fond of the child
Rough and uncouth, and always smelling of drink
vs.why: Grizzled hair and whiskers and “a perpetual smell of drink.” Perpetual — not now and then. He is drunk twice in the few weeks she is there, and that is only what she sees.

vs.q: What does Mr. Rucastle do about Toller’s drinking?
opts: He dismisses him on the spot
He takes no notice of it
He locks the drink away
He has his wife keep him out of sight
vs.why: “Twice since I have been with them he has been drunk, and yet Mr. Rucastle seemed to take no notice of it.” A master who ignores that is a master who needs this particular servant more than he needs him sober.

vs.q: What is Toller’s wife like?
opts: Kind, and glad of another woman in the house
Talkative, and full of the family’s history
Tall and strong, with a sour face, and silent
Frail, and seldom seen downstairs
vs.why: “As silent as Mrs. Rucastle, and much less amiable.” Two silent women in one house, and Miss Hunter notices that both of them are silent rather than only one.

vs.q: Why does it matter that the household is so small?
opts: It explains why the salary is so high
It shows the Rucastles cannot afford to keep more
Fewer people means fewer who could see or tell anything
It means Miss Hunter must do the cooking
vs.why: A big house, a locked wing, a dog loose at night, and two servants — one of them usually drunk and the other sour and silent. Whatever is being kept quiet here is being kept quiet by a very short list of people.

hi: laid upon the bed in your room
signs of having been worn before
a better fit if I had been measured for it
with its back turned towards it

vs.q: What is Miss Hunter asked to do on her third day?
opts: Take the child out to the lawn
Clean the rooms in the empty wing
Put on the electric blue dress
Read to Mrs. Rucastle in the drawing room
vs.why: The dress is already laid out on her bed when she is asked — the request and the preparation arrive together, which is how everything at this house works.

vs.q: What does she notice about the dress itself?
opts: It was far too large for her
It had plainly been worn before, and fitted her perfectly
It was brand new, and still had the shop label on it
It was the wrong shade of blue entirely
vs.why: Both at once. Somebody else wore this dress, and it fits Miss Hunter as though she had been measured for it — which is a thing to hold on to when you remember that she was chosen on sight.

vs.q: How is the chair arranged in the drawing room?
opts: Facing the fire, away from the door
Close to the central window, with its back to it
In the middle of the room, facing the door
Beside Mrs. Rucastle, at the far end
vs.why: Back to the window. She cannot see out, and anyone outside can see her. Everything that follows — the mirror, the man on the road — comes from that one arrangement.

vs.q: What is Mrs. Rucastle doing while her husband tells his funny stories?
opts: Laughing harder than anybody
Reading quietly by the fire
Sitting with her hands in her lap, looking sad
Out of the room altogether, on some errand
vs.why: He is working hard to make Miss Hunter laugh; his wife sits through it “with a sad, anxious look upon her face” and never smiles once. One of these two people is pretending and the other cannot.

vs.q: Put the three together — the borrowed dress, the chair at the window, the laughing. What is the performance for?
opts: To cheer Mrs. Rucastle up
To test whether Miss Hunter is good company
To be seen from outside the house
To keep the child amused in the next room
vs.why: She is dressed in another woman’s clothes, placed where the window frames her, and made to laugh. Nothing about it is for the people in the room — and Miss Hunter works that out herself two pages later.

hi: this same performance was gone through
begged me to read aloud to him
I read for about ten minutes
ordered me to cease and change my dress

vs.q: How often does the window performance happen?
opts: Once only, on her third day
Every morning without fail
Twice — and then it stops
Every evening after the child is in bed
vs.why: The third day, then two days later, and after the man on the road is waved away it never happens again. Two performances, and then the blind comes down for good.

vs.q: What does Mr. Rucastle add the second time?
opts: He asks her to sing
He hands her a novel and asks her to read aloud
He brings the child in to sit beside her chair
He moves the chair to face the window
vs.why: He gives her a book and moves her chair a little sideways. The sideways move is the detail: he is adjusting the picture, not the reading.

vs.q: How long does the reading last?
opts: All afternoon
About an hour
About ten minutes
Until the child woke from his nap
vs.why: Ten minutes, and then he orders her to stop and change. Nobody who wanted a novel read to them stops after ten minutes — the reading is a way of keeping her sitting there, nothing more.

vs.q: What word does Miss Hunter use for what Mr. Rucastle does when the reading is over?
opts: He asked her to change
He suggested that she change
He ordered her to cease and change
He thanked her and left the room
vs.why: Ordered. Everywhere else he is jovial and coaxing; here the mask slips for a word. She reports the exact verb, which is what makes her a good witness.

vs.q: Why does Miss Hunter call it a “performance”?
opts: Because the stories were so well told
Because Mrs. Rucastle treated it as a joke
Because it was staged, and repeated the same way
Because the child watched from the doorway
vs.why: Same dress, same chair, same window, same laughter, done twice “under exactly similar circumstances.” A thing arranged and run through again is a performance, and she names it correctly before she knows why.

missions.name: Section 2 — pages 188 to 190
missions.blurb: The piece of broken mirror, the man on the road, and Carlo

hi: turn my face away from the window
My hand mirror had been broken
There was nothing
a small bearded man in a grey suit

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter want to know, and why can she not simply look?
opts: What is in the locked drawer; it is locked
What is behind her; they always turn her face from the window
What is in the empty wing; the door is barred
Who the child is so frightened of; the boy will not say
vs.why: “They were always careful to turn my face away from the window.” Being carefully prevented from looking is itself a piece of information, and it is what makes her determined to see.

vs.q: How does she manage to see behind her?
opts: She moves the chair when nobody is watching
She asks the child to tell her what is outside
She hides a piece of broken mirror in her handkerchief
She watches the reflection in the window glass instead
vs.why: Her hand mirror had broken, so she keeps a sliver of it in her handkerchief and raises the handkerchief to her eyes in the middle of her laughter. She improvises, and she hides it inside something she is already doing.

vs.q: What does she see the first time she looks?
opts: A man on the road
The mastiff loose on the lawn
Nothing
Toller watching from the kitchen door
vs.why: “There was nothing.” The story lets the trick fail first. It is only at the second glance that she picks the man out — which is what looking properly is like.

vs.q: Who is in the road?
opts: Toller, walking back from the village
A small bearded man in a grey suit
A policeman from Winchester
The child’s former nurse
vs.why: A small bearded man in a grey suit, leaning on the railings and looking earnestly. The road is a busy highway, so a man on it is ordinary — a man stopped and staring at one window is not.

vs.q: What makes this man different from anyone else who passes on that road?
opts: He is dressed a good deal better than the local people
He is standing still, and looking earnestly at her window
He is carrying something under his arm
He waves as soon as he sees her
vs.why: “The road is an important highway, and there are usually people there.” She rules out the ordinary explanation herself before drawing any conclusion, which is exactly how Holmes would have done it.

hi: her eyes fixed upon me with a searching gaze
there is a fellow upon the road who stares up at Miss Hunter
Kindly turn round and motion him to go away
drew down the blind

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter notice when she lowers the handkerchief?
opts: That the man in the road had gone
That Mr. Rucastle had stopped telling his funny story
That Mrs. Rucastle’s eyes were fixed on her, searching
That the child had come into the room
vs.why: She catches Mrs. Rucastle watching her at the exact moment she is doing something she should not. The watcher is being watched, and both of them know it.

vs.q: What does Mrs. Rucastle say to her husband?
opts: That Miss Hunter has a mirror
That a fellow on the road is staring up at Miss Hunter
That the blind ought to be drawn
That the blue dress does not suit Miss Hunter at all
vs.why: Notice what she does not say. She has just worked out that Miss Hunter has seen the road, and she reports the man rather than the mirror — she gets the window shut without admitting what she knows.

vs.q: What is Miss Hunter told to do about the man?
opts: To ignore him and go on reading
To go out and ask him his business
To turn round and wave him away
To draw the blind herself
vs.why: And she objects first: “Surely it would be better to take no notice?” She is told again, and does it. The gesture has to come from her, in that dress, at that window.

vs.q: What changes after that day?
opts: She is moved to a different room
The man in the grey suit comes back again every afternoon
She never sits in the window or wears the dress again
Mr. Rucastle stops speaking to her
vs.why: All three at once, and she lists them in one breath. Whatever the performance was for, it was finished the moment that man was waved away.

vs.q: Why would waving him away be the point of the whole performance?
opts: It proves to him that she is happy there
It tells him, in her person, that he should stop coming
It gives Mrs. Rucastle an excuse to shut the blind
It shows the Rucastles that she will obey them
vs.why: A man waits by the railings to see a particular woman at that window. He is shown a woman in her dress, laughing, who turns and waves him off — and he does not come back. He has been answered by someone he thinks is somebody else.

hi: the rattling of a chain
so that he is always keen
Toller lets him loose every night
a giant dog, as large as a calf

vs.q: What is kept in the outbuilding near the kitchen door?
opts: The Rucastles’ carriage horse
Carlo, a mastiff
The photographic equipment
Firewood and garden tools
vs.why: She hears a chain rattling and something large moving before she is shown anything. The dog is introduced by sound first, which is how it is remembered.

vs.q: Who is the only person who can handle the dog?
opts: Mr. Rucastle, who calls him his own
Mrs. Rucastle
Old Toller
Nobody — he is left alone entirely
vs.why: “I call him mine, but really old Toller is the only man who can do anything with him.” Which is worth putting beside the fact that Toller is drunk a good deal of the time.

vs.q: Why is the dog fed only once a day, and not much then?
opts: So that he stays thin enough to run
Because food is short in the house
So that he is always keen
Because he will take food from nobody else
vs.why: Keen means hungry and ready. The dog is kept hungry on purpose, which turns an animal into a thing with a job — and the job is announced in the next sentence.

vs.q: What is Miss Hunter warned never to do?
opts: Go into the empty wing
Open the locked drawer
Set foot outside at night
Speak to anyone on the road
vs.why: “For goodness’ sake don’t ever set your foot over the threshold at night.” Said as kindly advice. It is also, exactly, a way of making sure she cannot leave the house after dark.

vs.q: What does she see from her bedroom window two nights later?
opts: Mr. Rucastle crossing the lawn with a lamp
The man in the grey suit at the railings
A giant dog, as large as a calf, crossing the moonlit lawn
Toller letting somebody in quietly at the kitchen door
vs.why: “That dreadful sight sent a chill to my heart, which I do not think any burglar could have done.” She had been told; seeing it is different, and she says so plainly.

missions.name: Section 3 — pages 191 to 194
missions.blurb: Her own hair in a locked drawer, and the wing she may not enter

hi: a great coil at the bottom of my trunk
the lower one locked
It was my coil of hair
they were identical

vs.q: What had Miss Hunter done with the hair she cut off in London?
opts: Sold it before she left
Thrown it away at her lodging
Packed it in a coil at the bottom of her trunk
Given it away to Miss Stoper at the agency
vs.why: She kept it — and kept it at the bottom of a trunk in her own room, which is what makes the next few minutes impossible rather than merely odd.

vs.q: How does she come to open the locked drawer?
opts: She finds the key left in the lock
She needs the space, and one of her own keys fits
Mrs. Rucastle asks her to empty it out
The drawer had been left standing open by mistake
vs.why: Two drawers full, more to pack, and a third locked. She assumes it was fastened by mistake and tries her own keys — “the very first key fit to perfection.” She is not snooping; she is unpacking.

vs.q: What is in the drawer?
opts: A photograph of a young woman
A coil of hair exactly like her own
The large black linen bag
A bundle of letters, tied with tape
vs.why: One thing only. The same peculiar chestnut tint, the same thickness — and her own coil is still at the bottom of her trunk where she left it.

vs.q: How does she check that it is not her own hair?
opts: She counts the pins that were in it
She asks Toller’s wife whose it is
She fetches her own from the trunk and lays them together
She looks for the ribbon that she had tied her own with
vs.why: She does not guess and she does not panic. She goes and gets the other one and puts them side by side — “I assure you they were identical.” That is an experiment.

vs.q: Why does she say nothing to the Rucastles about it?
opts: She was afraid of the mastiff
She thought they would not believe her
She felt she had put herself in the wrong by opening a locked drawer
She had promised the servants that she would keep it all quiet
vs.why: Scrupulous, even here. She has found something frightening and her first thought is that she had no business in that drawer. It costs her — she now has to carry it alone.

hi: one wing, however, that appeared not to be inhabited
a very different person from the jovial man
the veins stood out at his temples
The fourth was shuttered up

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter say about her own habits of mind?
opts: That she is too curious for her own good
That she is naturally observant
That she is slow to take alarm
That she forgets names and faces easily
vs.why: “I am naturally observant, Mr. Holmes, and I soon had a pretty good plan of the whole house in my head.” She says it as a plain fact about herself, and the reading keeps proving it.

vs.q: What does she notice about one wing of the house?
opts: It has been newly painted
It is not lived in, and its door is always locked
It is where the Tollers sleep
It can only be reached from the garden on the outside
vs.why: A door opposite the Tollers’ quarters, always locked. In a house with two servants and empty rooms everywhere, one wing is locked — and the lock is the interesting part.

vs.q: How does Mr. Rucastle look when she meets him coming out of that door?
opts: Exactly as jovial as always
Tired, as though he had been working hard
Red-faced and furious, quite unlike himself
Frightened, and in a great hurry
vs.why: Cheeks red, brow crinkled with anger, veins standing out at his temples — “a very different person from the jovial man to whom I was accustomed.” It is the first time she sees what is under the laughing.

vs.q: What does he do when he passes her on the stair?
opts: Explains what he had been doing
Locks the door and hurries past without a word or a look
Asks her what she is doing upstairs
Drops his keys on the stair, and she picks them up for him
