vs.why: He locks it first. Even in a rage, the door gets locked — and he cannot manage a word to her, which from this man is as loud as shouting.

vs.q: What does she see when she goes round to look at that wing’s windows?
opts: All four boarded over
Lights burning in two of the four windows
Three simply dirty, the fourth shuttered up
Bars across every one
vs.why: Three dirty windows say nobody lives there. One shuttered window says somebody has gone to trouble over that room in particular — and she will meet the inside of it two pages later.

hi: Photography is one of my hobbies
there was no jest in his eyes
a feeling of duty
a large black linen bag

vs.q: What does Mr. Rucastle say the shuttered room is for?
opts: Storing furniture
A darkroom for his photography
A nursery, no longer in use
He refuses to say at all
vs.why: Photography, he says — and a darkroom does need a shuttered window, so the explanation fits the one fact she has mentioned. It does not fit the bar from an iron bed, which she has not seen yet.

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter notice about the way he says it?
opts: He stammered over the word darkroom
He would not look at her at all
He spoke jokingly, but there was no jest in his eyes
He laughed so hard that he could not finish it
vs.why: “I read suspicion there, and annoyance, but no jest.” She separates the tone from the eyes. That is a skill, and it is the same one that catches the voice being “a little too coaxing” later.

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter say her wish to see the rooms is, if it is not curiosity?
opts: A wish to prove Holmes right
A feeling of duty — that some good might come of it
A hope of finding something worth money
Fear of being blamed later if something happened
vs.why: “It was not mere curiosity. It was more a feeling of duty — a feeling that some good might come from my penetrating to this place.” She is not sure where the feeling comes from and says so honestly.

vs.q: What has she seen Mr. Rucastle carry through the forbidden door?
opts: A tray of food
A lamp and a bundle of candles
A large black linen bag
The coil of hair from the drawer
vs.why: One detail, dropped in among others. She reports it without saying what she thinks it means — which is the right way round, and makes it worth more.

vs.q: What finally gives her the chance to go in?
opts: Mrs. Rucastle takes the child away for a day
She finds a spare key in the drawer
Toller gets very drunk, and the key is left in the door
The Tollers both go into Winchester for the evening
vs.why: Everything at once: Toller drunk, the key in the door, both Rucastles downstairs with the child. The chance is made by the one servant who can be relied on being unreliable.

missions.name: Section 4 — pages 195 to 198
missions.blurb: Behind the barricaded door, and what Rucastle says while he is smiling

hi: three doors in a line
one of the broad bars of an iron bed
Evidently a skylight let in light from above
saw a shadow pass back and forth

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter find round the corner of the passage?
opts: A staircase leading down to the cellar
Three doors in a line, two of them open
A single door, standing wide
A corridor of locked bedrooms
vs.why: The first and third lead into empty rooms, dusty and cheerless. Only the middle one is shut — and the two open ones are there so that you notice the shut one.

vs.q: How is the middle door fastened?
opts: With a padlock and chain through the handle
Nailed shut from the outside
With a bar from an iron bed, padlocked and corded across it
Only locked, in the same way as every other door up there
vs.why: Padlocked to a ring in the wall at one end, tied with heavy cord at the other, and the door locked as well. That is not how you secure a darkroom. It is how you secure a person.

vs.q: What tells her the room beyond is not dark?
opts: A lamp burning under the door
A glimmer under the door, from a skylight above
The shutter had been opened
She can hear somebody striking a match in there
vs.why: Light from above, which the shuttered window cannot explain. The one room they have blacked out from outside has light coming into it from the roof — so the shutter is not there to keep light out.

vs.q: What does she hear and see while she stands there?
opts: Nothing at all, which is why she left
Someone calling out to her through the door
Steps inside, and a shadow passing back and forth
Toller coming up the stairs behind her
vs.why: Somebody is walking up and down in that room. That is the moment the house stops being strange and becomes something worse, and she says so: “a mad, unreasoning terror rose up in me.”

vs.q: Put the bar, the skylight and the footsteps together. What has she found?
opts: A darkroom in use
A storeroom nobody has opened in years
A room with somebody shut inside it
An empty room the Rucastles are afraid of
vs.why: Barred from the outside, lit from above, and with somebody walking about inside. Every one of those three facts is in front of her, and the conclusion needs nothing else.

hi: I thought it must be when I saw the door open
just a little too coaxing
He overdid it
to keep people out who have no business there

vs.q: Who is waiting outside the door when she runs out?
opts: Toller’s wife
Mr. Rucastle
Mrs. Rucastle, with the child
Nobody — she gets back to her room unseen
vs.why: She runs straight into his arms. He had seen the door open and worked out who it must be — so he was waiting, and he let her go all the way in first.

vs.q: How does Mr. Rucastle speak to her at first?
opts: Angrily, demanding an explanation
Coldly, saying nothing at all
In a caressing, soothing manner
He laughs and makes a joke of it
vs.why: “My dear young lady! my dear young lady!” It is kindness turned up as far as it will go, applied to a woman he has just caught in the one place he forbade.

vs.q: What does Miss Hunter make of that manner?
opts: That he was genuinely concerned for her
That it was a little too coaxing — he overdid it
That he had not understood where she had been
That he was about to dismiss her
vs.why: “He overdid it. I was keenly on my guard against him.” She reads the excess rather than the warmth, which is the second time this reading that she catches him acting.

vs.q: What does she tell him, and what does she keep back?
opts: Everything, including the footsteps
That she went into the empty wing and the stillness frightened her
Nothing at all — she refuses to answer him so much as a word
That she was looking for the child
vs.why: True, and not the whole truth. She says nothing about the barred door or the shadow — and his “Only that?” shows he is testing exactly that gap.

vs.q: What reason does he give for locking the door?
opts: That the floor is unsafe up there
That his photographs would all be spoiled
To keep people out who have no business there
That his wife asked him to
vs.why: Said “still smiling in the most amiable manner.” It explains nothing — every locked door keeps people out — and it is the last thing he says before the smile goes.

hi: the smile hardened into a grin of rage
I’ll throw you to the mastiff
even of the child
my curiosity was almost as strong as my fears

vs.q: What does Mr. Rucastle say if she goes through that door again?
opts: That she will be dismissed at once
That he will write to Miss Stoper
That he will throw her to the mastiff
That he will lock her in her room
vs.why: And the smile “hardened into a grin of rage” as he said it. A dog kept hungry on purpose, and a man who has just named it as a punishment for her.

vs.q: What happens to his manner as he says it?
opts: He keeps smiling throughout
He turns away so she cannot see his face
The smile hardens into a grin of rage
He begins to laugh, as at a joke
vs.why: The jovial man and the furious one are the same face, and she watches it change in a single sentence. It is the clearest look at him in the whole reading.

vs.q: Who is Miss Hunter frightened of by the end?
opts: Only Mr. Rucastle
Mr. Rucastle and Toller
The house, the man, the woman, the servants, even the child
Nobody at all — she says that her nerve had quite returned
vs.why: She lists them, and the list ends “even of the child.” The whole house has become frightening, not one person in it.

vs.q: Why does she not simply run away?
opts: She has nowhere to go and no money
She had promised to stay the quarter
Her curiosity was almost as strong as her fears
The mastiff is loose on the lawn at night
vs.why: “Of course I might have fled, but my curiosity was almost as strong as my fears.” Almost — she is honest that the fear is the bigger of the two, and she stays anyway.

vs.q: What does she decide to do instead?
opts: Confront Mr. Rucastle about the room
Send for Sherlock Holmes
Ask the servants what is behind the door
Take the child and leave in the night
vs.why: “Then I thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not live there longer without some advice.” It is why she is sitting in the Black Swan telling him all this, and where tonight’s reading stops.
